title: Are You Better Off?

jokes.text: Ron's grumbling about 'lending' his cabin: 'Makes it sound like I had a choice in the matter. I never should've agreed to this or let you know that I have a cabin or gotten to know any of you.'
jokes.setup: Leslie thanks Ron for 'lending' his cabin, implying generosity
jokes.punchline: Ron escalates from complaining about the word 'lending' to regretting knowing any of his colleagues — classic Ron misanthropy
jokes.explanation: This is quintessential Ron Swanson. The escalating regret ('or let you know that I have a cabin / or gotten to know any of you') is perfectly structured, character-specific, and deeply quotable. Only Ron could deliver this with a straight face and make it warm rather than cruel. The structure is a triple-beat escalation that lands harder each step.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Thank you so much for lending us your cabin, Ron. It was perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You're welcome.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Actually, I regret that.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I regret lending you the cabin.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I regret telling you I had a cabin.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I regret ever meeting you.

jokes.text: Leslie asks what makes Pawnee great; April answers: 'Easy: Most murders per capita. The guillotine was invented here. City Hall is run by the walrus mafia.'
jokes.setup: Leslie prompts a cheerful civic-pride brainstorm about Pawnee's greatness
jokes.punchline: April responds with a deadpan list of increasingly disturbing and absurd 'facts' about Pawnee
jokes.explanation: The 'walrus mafia' is the peak of this — absurdist enough to be genuinely funny rather than just dark. April's complete sincerity in delivery makes it work. Each item escalates in absurdity nicely. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Pawnee Founder's Week is the most magical time of the year! The parade is going to be absolutely spectacular. We've got floats, marching bands, confetti cannons...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's basically the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, except better because it's in Pawnee.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It looks like a turds-on-wheels convention.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, you're being deliberately negative. This is a celebration of our town's heritage!

jokes.text: Donna reveals she has a condo in Seattle: 'Yes, I like the rain and the fish markets.' — delivered as a completely casual non-sequitur
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Donna what makes Pawnee great; Donna's answer is that it's cheap enough to save for her real home elsewhere
jokes.punchline: Donna has a whole separate life planned in Seattle, referenced with total nonchalance
jokes.explanation: Donna's secret double life is a funny reveal — she's so unbothered by Pawnee that she's been quietly planning her exit. The specificity of 'the rain and the fish markets' adds dry texture. Good character work.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Our history of incredibly low standards and a complete lack of self-awareness.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Also, we have the lowest life expectancy in the state, so you don't have to worry about getting old here.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Plus, our water tastes like a tire fire, which gives you something to look forward to every morning.

jokes.text: 'I'm bored. Let's go have sex in a tree.' Andy to April, mid-meeting, with complete sincerity
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to refocus the group on Founder's Week brainstorming
jokes.punchline: Andy suggests having sex in a tree as the alternative, treating it as a completely reasonable proposal
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Andy — the total non-sequitur delivered as practical problem-solving. Short, specific, and character-perfect. The tree detail is the key; it elevates beyond generic Andy horndog into something specific and weird.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What makes Pawnee great, Donna?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm outta here. I got a job offer in Indianapolis, and I'm taking it. Pawnee's great because of people like you, Leslie. But I need to do what's best for me now.

jokes.text: Leslie, resignedly: 'He'll be back in eight minutes.'
jokes.setup: Andy and April leave to have sex in a tree
jokes.punchline: Leslie's completely unfazed prediction — she knows exactly how long this will take — implies she's been through this before and has timed it
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional economy — four words that contain a layered joke (Leslie has timed Andy's sexual encounters, which is both absurd and a damning commentary on Andy), delivered as resigned workplace management. Maximum funny per word. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, what? You have a secret life?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Leslie, I'm a woman of mystery. I have three different retirement accounts, a boat I keep in Muncie, and I've been taking salsa lessons for six years.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: How did I not know any of this?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Because you don't ask. You just assume everyone's life is as open as yours, which it ain't.

jokes.text: Andy calls back from offscreen: 'Anyone's welcome to join us in the tree!'
jokes.setup: Andy and April have just left to have sex in a tree
jokes.punchline: Andy extends a cheerful, open invitation to his coworkers to join them

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa Saperstein
dialogue.line: We should have a parade, but instead of floats, we use actual dead animals. And we stuff them with candy so kids can hit them with sticks.

jokes.text: Ben finds a pregnancy test in Ron's trash while retrieving his sweatshirt, then adds: 'Side note: I accidentally threw my sweat shirt away. That's why I was digging through the trash. Found that too. Pretty cool.'
jokes.setup: Ben has found a pregnancy test and is building to a dramatic announcement
jokes.punchline: He derails himself to explain the embarrassing sweatshirt story and then casually celebrates retrieving it
jokes.explanation: The self-undermining confession mid-dramatic-revelation is well-structured. 'Pretty cool' as the kicker for recovering a sweatshirt from trash is perfectly deflating. Good economy and character work — Ben's bumbling earnestness is on full display.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: They'll be done in seven minutes.

jokes.text: Ben launches into his 'Bert Macklin, FBI' alter ego with full commitment: 'They said I was retired. They said I was too dangerous for the Pawnee Police Department. Turns out they were right...and wrong. Macklin, you son of a bitch.'
jokes.setup: Ben has found a pregnancy test and decides to investigate who is pregnant
jokes.punchline: He invents an FBI persona, delivers a hard-boiled monologue to himself in a mirror/camera, and calls himself 'son of a bitch'
jokes.explanation: Wait — this is Andy's running Bert Macklin character, not Ben's. The joke works because Andy is treating a mundane pregnancy mystery as a high-stakes FBI thriller with total sincerity. 'Macklin, you son of a bitch' directed at himself in the mirror is an iconic Parks moment. High quotability and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Because she wanted to come. I don't make decisions. I just drive her places and buy things.

jokes.text: Leslie's announcement: 'Due to a tragic misunderstanding, the prettiest pig beauty pageant has been replaced by a pork rib barbecue competition.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is cheerfully announcing Founder's Week events
jokes.punchline: The pigs entered in the beauty pageant were apparently eaten — referenced only as a 'tragic misunderstanding' with zero further elaboration
jokes.explanation: This is a masterclass in economy and dark comedy. The entire horrifying implication is conveyed in one sentence, with 'tragic misunderstanding' doing all the heavy lifting. The pivot to 'on to less grisly news' confirms the dark reading without belaboring it. Sharp, original, and perfectly deadpan. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I was looking for my shirt. I accidentally threw it away with Ron's trash, and I was just trying to get it back.

jokes.text: The announcer's follow-up: 'on to less grisly news' — implicitly confirming the pigs were turned into ribs
jokes.setup: The prettiest pig pageant became a rib competition
jokes.punchline: 'Less grisly news' acknowledges with perfect understatement that yes, those were the same pigs

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I am Bert Macklin, FBI. And I'm on the case. A pregnancy test. Left here. In the bathroom. Who could it belong to? Was it Ann? Was it Leslie? Was it... me? No. No, it wasn't me. I'm a man.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'our parade makes the rose bowl parade look like a turds-on-wheels convention.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is hyping Founder's Week
jokes.punchline: 'Turds-on-wheels convention' is the specific, disgusting, unexpected image she lands on as the insult comparison
jokes.explanation: The absurd specificity of 'turds-on-wheels convention' is very Parks and Rec — Leslie's civic boosterism expressed through a surprisingly crude but precise image. The confidence of the delivery makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Announcer
dialogue.line: Due to budget cuts, this year's Founder's Week pageant will no longer feature live pigs. The pigs have been... reassigned to other city departments.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Whoa! Darren! Slow down! That sweat suit's not for sweatin' in, okay? This is crushed velvet. If you go at more than a brisk walk, it will fall apart.'
jokes.setup: Tom has set up a rental clothing store; a customer is wearing a velvet sweat suit
jokes.punchline: The sweat suit is purely decorative — it cannot withstand actual exercise. Tom's horror at the functional use of athletic wear is peak Tom
jokes.explanation: Tom panicking about crushed velvet being used for actual sweating is perfect character comedy. His priorities — aesthetics over function — are crystallized in this moment. 'Not for sweatin' in' is a great line.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Nobody's complaining. People love the new system. I haven't heard a single—

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: This is the worst thing that's ever happened!

jokes.text: Tom suggests 'Li'l Swaggers' for a baby section and 'Rent-A-Sag' for elderly clothing, then immediately: 'Ugh, no. Old people are gross.'
jokes.setup: Tom is excitedly brainstorming expansion plans for Rent-A-Swag
jokes.punchline: He comes up with 'Rent-A-Sag,' is briefly proud of it, then dismisses elderly customers as 'gross' — the wordplay and the self-sabotage land together
jokes.explanation: 'Rent-A-Sag' is a genuinely good pun, and Tom's immediate rejection of his own demographic expansion idea because old people are gross is classic character comedy. The self-awareness is funny — he knows it's a good name and rejects it anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: These shorts are made from a special moisture-wicking fabric.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: Great, so they'll keep me dry when I work out?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, no. If you actually exercise in them, they'll disintegrate. But you'll look amazing standing still.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: That doesn't make sense.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Welcome to high fashion, my friend.

jokes.text: Mona-Lisa: 'Hey, dingdong! Can I go home? My tum-tum feels gross, and also, I hate working.'
jokes.setup: Mona-Lisa is working at Rent-A-Swag, apparently as Tom's assistant
jokes.punchline: She gives two reasons to leave: a vague physical complaint expressed in baby talk, and a frank admission that she hates working — the second is the real one
jokes.explanation: 'Tum-tum feels gross' is a great Mona-Lisa-ism — she speaks like a toddler while being a fully grown adult. The addition of 'I hate working' as an equal co-reason is the punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, so I'm thinking about expanding Rent-A-Swag. We could do Rent-A-Sag for elderly people who need clothes that fit their... saggy situations.

jokes.text: Mona-Lisa: 'Also, a lawyer guy called you. He sounded really sexy on the phone, and I was very into that. Like, I was, like, very into that.'
jokes.setup: Mona-Lisa is relaying a business message to Tom
jokes.punchline: She completely derails the message to share her inappropriate attraction to the lawyer, repeating herself with escalating enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: Mona-Lisa's oversharing is a reliable comedic device. The repetition ('I was, like, very into that') mirrors how she processes her own feelings out loud, which is character-specific and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm thinking about expanding Tom's Bistro to cater to the elderly demographic. Early bird specials, soft foods, large print menus...

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: That's actually not a bad idea, Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Right? I could call it 'Señor Senior's' or something—

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Hard pass.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Let's set up some boundaries on what's cool for you to say to me.' Mona-Lisa immediately responds: 'Okay. I frenched my cousin one time.' / 'That's gross.' / 'I might still be in love with him.'
jokes.setup: Tom tries to establish professional boundaries
jokes.punchline: Mona-Lisa's response to the concept of 'boundaries' is to immediately share a progressively more disturbing overshare about her cousin
jokes.explanation: This is a perfectly structured three-beat escalation. Tom's sincere attempt to set professional norms is immediately destroyed. Each Mona-Lisa beat gets worse: (1) inappropriate revelation, (2) confirmed gross, (3) she might STILL be in love with him. The structure and character integration are exceptional — only Mona-Lisa could respond to 'let's set boundaries' this way. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa Saperstein
dialogue.line: This lawyer called me about some stuff, and his voice was so smooth. I got so into it that I asked him to keep talking about discovery motions just so I could hear him speak.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: That's... that's weird, Mona-Lisa.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa Saperstein
dialogue.line: I know! I told him I'd be his client for life. He seemed confused.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Babyface heard my demo? I will accept a record deal.' — responding to a lawyer contacting him about Rent-A-Swag
jokes.setup: A lawyer says his client is interested in making Tom an offer
jokes.punchline: Tom's first assumption is that a music producer wants to sign him as a recording artist
jokes.explanation: Tom's ego and side-hustle aspirations are perfectly captured. The specificity of 'Babyface' and 'I will accept' (not 'I'd be interested' but a formal declaration) is great character work.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Mona-Lisa, I need to set some boundaries. Please respect my personal space and privacy.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: Oh, no problem, Tom. I got it.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: By the way, I've been having this weird rash on my—

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, that's the boundary I just mentioned.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: Right, right. My bad. Hey, you wanna see pictures of my infected ingrown toenail?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No!

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: Well, I'm gonna describe it anyway. It's the size of a grape, and it's weeping this greenish—

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Stop! Why are you like this?

jokes.text: Tom repeatedly guesses the investor is Diddy despite the lawyer repeatedly denying it. Lawyer: 'It's not Diddy.' Tom: 'Got it.'
jokes.setup: Tom keeps guessing the mystery investor is a celebrity (Diddy)
jokes.punchline: The lawyer explicitly says 'It's not Diddy' — a sentence that should not need to be said — and Tom accepts it unconvincingly
jokes.explanation: The running Diddy gag across this episode is well-executed. The lawyer having to explicitly say 'It's not Diddy' is the funniest beat — that sentence existing in the world is inherently funny. Sets up a satisfying callback at episode's end.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: I have a client interested in your business.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Finally! Someone who appreciates real talent. Is it a record label? A management company? Are they ready to take Childish Gambino to the next level?

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: It's about your catering company.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh.

jokes.text: Andy (as Bert Macklin) approaches Ann with fake casualness, then: 'Congratulations.' Ann: 'Is that a question?' Andy: 'It's an accusation, 'cause I know your secret.'
jokes.setup: Andy is investigating who is pregnant, using his Bert Macklin FBI persona
jokes.punchline: He delivers 'Congratulations' as an 'accusation,' completely misunderstanding how either interrogation or accusations work

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: I can't tell you who the client is, but I can tell you it's not Diddy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So it's Diddy.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: No, it's definitely not Diddy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Why would you even bring up Diddy if it wasn't Diddy? Classic misdirect. It's Diddy.

jokes.text: Ann's reaction to learning someone is pregnant: 'I'm trying to get pregnant. That's not fair. I mean, great, and happy for them, and congratulations, whatever, but ooh! No! Boo!'
jokes.setup: Ann hears that someone else is pregnant while she's been trying
jokes.punchline: Her emotional whiplash — trying to be a good person, failing, cycling through performed happiness then genuine jealousy — all in one rapid-fire run
jokes.explanation: The speed of Ann's collapse from performing happiness to 'No! Boo!' is the joke. Relatable and well-performed. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Ann, I need to tell you something. I'm actually a highly trained FBI agent. I went through the whole program at Quantico.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Andy, no you didn't.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yes I did! I'm Bert Macklin, FBI. It's all real.

jokes.text: Andy (Macklin) says he works alone. Ann offers lunch with 'as many burgers as you want.' Andy: 'Welcome to the FBI.'
jokes.setup: Bert Macklin insists he works alone in a tough-guy FBI way
jokes.punchline: The entire principle is immediately abandoned for the promise of unlimited burgers

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Ann, I need to ask you something and I need you to be completely honest with me.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Okay... what?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Are you pregnant?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What? No!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Because I've been watching you very carefully, and you've been acting strange. You've been tired, you've been emotional, and you threw up in the bathroom this morning.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I have food poisoning, Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's what a pregnant person would say.

jokes.text: Ben's talking head about Pawnee's health improvements: 'Together, as a town, we lost an amount of weight equal to 800 pregnant manatees.'
jokes.setup: Ben is presenting health statistics to make Leslie look good
jokes.punchline: He uses 'pregnant manatees' as the unit of weight measurement — specific, aquatic, and oddly precise
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'pregnant manatees' as a weight unit is genuinely original and funny. It implies someone calculated this, which is its own absurdist joke. 'Pregnant' is the detail that pushes it from good to great.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh my god, that's wonderful! Congratulations! I'm so happy for you.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I mean, you're not even that pretty. How did you...? No, that's great. That's really great.

jokes.text: 'A gym opened, and it stayed in business.'
jokes.setup: Ben is listing Pawnee's health improvements
jokes.punchline: The bar for success is so low that a gym merely staying open is a remarkable civic achievement
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy — six words that convey the full depth of Pawnee's dysfunction. The joke works because it implies everything that came before: in Pawnee, gyms don't stay in business. Perfect deadpan understatement.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No, I'm not interested in any kind of partnership with you.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Not even if I throw in free waffles?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, yeah, let's be partners.

jokes.text: 'People checking into the E.R. after ingesting a whole candy wrapper is down 40%.'
jokes.setup: Continuing the list of health statistics
jokes.punchline: The existence of a measurable rate of Pawnee residents eating entire candy wrappers (and going to the E.R. for it) is the joke
jokes.explanation: The deadpan delivery of an absurd public health statistic is the show's bread and butter. 'Down 40%' implies it was astronomically high before. Strong Pawnee world-building humor.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm not partnering with you on this investigation. I work alone.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What if I throw in unlimited burgers?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Done. We're partners.

jokes.text: Pinewood's counter: 'You somehow convinced the school board that napkins are a vegetable.' Ben: 'They're made from plants.'
jokes.setup: Debate about Sweetums school lunches
jokes.punchline: Ben's defense of 'napkins are a vegetable' is technically accurate and completely wrong simultaneously
jokes.explanation: This is a standout joke. The absurdity of napkins-as-vegetables in school lunches is the setup, but the punchline — 'They're made from plants' — is delivered with such straight-faced logic that it becomes its own separate joke. The layered absurdism (the school board accepting it, Ben defending it with actual botany) earns an 8+. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie's health initiatives have actually made a real difference in this town. Sure, the results aren't perfect, but they're an improvement.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: An improvement? Ben, I've seen the new fitness center. It's a converted storage unit with a broken treadmill and a motivational poster of a crying eagle.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Okay, but last year there wasn't even a crying eagle.

jokes.text: Dewey from Sanitation: 'Ever since you stripped us of our freedoms by making us hire women, we've had to turn one of our bathrooms into a woman's bathroom. We only have one bathroom now.'
jokes.setup: Dewey is complaining about Leslie's unfair regulations
jokes.punchline: The 'freedom stripped' is having to include women in the workforce; the complaint is so reflexively sexist it satirizes itself
jokes.explanation: The joke lands through satire of male entitlement framed as freedom. The specificity of 'one bathroom' as the grievance is good. Fits the show's pattern of using Pawnee citizens to satirize real political attitudes.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: These lunches are completely unhealthy. There's no nutritional value whatsoever.

dialogue.speaker: Ms. Pinewood
dialogue.line: Well, we do serve vegetables.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What vegetables?

dialogue.speaker: Ms. Pinewood
dialogue.line: The napkins are made from processed cellulose, which comes from trees, which are plants.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I'm so sorry, Dewey. That sounds like a horrible price to pay for something as trivial as gender equality.' Dewey: 'So you agree.'
jokes.setup: Leslie responds to Dewey's bathroom complaint with maximum sarcasm
jokes.punchline: Dewey completely misses the sarcasm and takes her statement as agreement
jokes.explanation: Dewey's complete inability to detect sarcasm is the joke. Leslie's escalating exasperation at being misunderstood is a reliable comedic engine for the show.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Leslie's policies are destroying this department. She's treating everyone equally, as if we're all the same.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Yeah, man, it's crazy. I used to get special treatment.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Exactly. Now I'm expected to follow the same rules as everyone else. It's oppression.

jokes.text: Bjorn Lerpiss complains that the park replaced a planned Paunch Burger: 'Now, if I wanna start my day off with a triple-decker pancake breakfast pizza, I gotta go to the one that's 10 minutes away, and that makes me 20 minutes late to work every day.' Leslie: 'I work at home.'
jokes.setup: Bjorn complains about a 10-minute commute to his nearest fast food being an enormous hardship
jokes.punchline: He works from home — the commute excuse is completely destroyed
jokes.explanation: Well-constructed two-beat joke: the absurdity of 'triple-decker pancake breakfast pizza' sets up Pawnee's food culture, then the punchline destroys his only logical grievance. 'I work at home' is a perfect, short kicker. Good structure.

dialogue.speaker: Dewey
dialogue.line: This bathroom situation is unfair to men. Women get a dedicated bathroom, but we have to share.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh yes, Dewey. Gender equality. Such a trivial issue.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Have you ever considered not eating that for breakfast?' Bjorn: 'I'll never consider that.'
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to suggest a simple behavioral change
jokes.punchline: Bjorn's flat, absolute refusal — not 'I can't' but 'I'll never consider that' — is both funny and somehow principled

dialogue.speaker: Bjorn
dialogue.line: I can't believe you're replacing the McDonald's with a park. Where am I supposed to get lunch now?

dialogue.speaker: Parks Department Official
dialogue.line: Don't you work from home?

dialogue.speaker: Bjorn
dialogue.line: Yes, but...

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head: 'This feels strangely personal. Maybe it's because they're all standing up saying how much they hate me as a person.'
jokes.setup: A parade of citizens has been publicly criticizing Leslie
jokes.punchline: Her deadpan assessment that it 'feels strangely personal' undercuts the enormousness of the public humiliation
jokes.explanation: Classic Leslie — refusing to acknowledge the full emotional weight of being attacked, then immediately acknowledging the full emotional weight. Good character voice.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We could try the oatmeal. It's actually really good for you.

dialogue.speaker: Bjorn
dialogue.line: No. Eggs only. Eggs for breakfast, eggs for lunch, eggs for dinner. I will not betray the egg.

jokes.text: Andy (as Macklin) asks Donna: 'How many people am I talking to, Donna? One or 1 1/9?'
jokes.setup: Bert Macklin is interrogating Donna about whether she's pregnant, trying to be subtle
jokes.punchline: '1 and 1/9' as a way to ask if someone is pregnant — treating pregnancy as a mathematical fraction of personhood — is a strange and specific piece of Andy logic
jokes.explanation: This is a standout joke. '1 or 1 1/9' is such a specific, weird, and somehow logical piece of Andy-math that it's genuinely original. The fraction implies a fetus is 1/9 of a person, which is wrong in every sense but internally consistent for Andy. Highly quotable and distinctive. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Donna, I have a math question. If a woman was expecting something, how would you know?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Andy, what are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Just hypothetically. Like, what are the nine... I mean, what are the signs?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Are you asking me if I'm pregnant?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What? No! I'm just really into math right now. You know what they call nine months? The sum of all my fears.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I'm not pregnant, you idiot.

jokes.text: Donna's response to Macklin's question: 'I'm a grown woman with a good head on her shoulders. Don't worry about me.'
jokes.setup: Andy is being transparently obvious about asking if she's pregnant
jokes.punchline: Donna dismisses the entire line of questioning with total self-assurance, neither confirming nor denying anything
jokes.explanation: Good Donna moment — her refusal to engage is characterful. But it's more of a grace note than a full joke.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I've been investigating this case for weeks, and I think I've finally cracked it. The perpetrator is obviously someone with a very low IQ, probably like a real idiot... I mean, not an idiot, just someone who makes idiotic decisions. What I'm trying to say is... they're dumb. No wait, that's worse. They're... intellectually challenged in a criminal way.

jokes.text: Donna: 'I don't remember saying anything about anyone being pregnant.' — Ben's reaction beat: 'Oh. Interesting.'
jokes.setup: Donna asks if Ben is asking her if she's pregnant; Ben denies it
jokes.punchline: Donna's sharp deflection, followed by Ben's 'Oh. Interesting.' treating her denial as a clue
jokes.explanation: Good small moment — Donna's 'I don't remember saying anything about anyone being pregnant' is a clever deflection that inadvertently reveals she understood exactly what was being asked. Ben's 'Oh. Interesting.' treating it as investigative gold is a good Macklin beat.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: This town has gone to hell. Moral decline, deteriorating values, people dressing like they don't care anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: We've really gone to hell in a hand basket. And not even a nice hand basket.

jokes.text: Andy's self-correction in his talking head: 'Whew. This case just got interesting. Well, not just. It was pretty interesting to begin with. This case just remained interesting.'
jokes.setup: Andy is dramatically narrating his investigation
jokes.punchline: He catches himself on the cliché and pedantically corrects it, which is funnier than if he'd just said the cliché
jokes.explanation: This subverts the TV detective trope by having Andy be unexpectedly precise about his own narration. The pedantry is funny because it's not an Andy trait — he's usually completely unconcerned with accuracy. The self-correction landing on 'remained interesting' is a perfect deflation.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So what kind of business are you in?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Pornography.

jokes.text: Man at forum: 'a year ago, this town was not a horrifying sex den where people could put their body parts anywhere they want with impunity. And then, you were elected. And now, this town is a horrifying sex den...'
jokes.setup: Citizen is complaining about comprehensive sex education
jokes.punchline: His description of Pawnee as a 'horrifying sex den' is wildly hyperbolic; he believes it sincerely and the crowd agrees
jokes.explanation: The repetition of 'horrifying sex den' and the phrase 'put their body parts anywhere they want with impunity' is funny for its pearl-clutching absurdity. Good satirical material.

dialogue.speaker: Brandi
dialogue.line: I've been in a lot of films. Like, a LOT of films. I was in a porn parody of 'Argo' called 'Our Goo.'

jokes.text: 'This town is going to hell in a Gucci knock-off handbag, girl.'
jokes.setup: Citizen is complaining about moral decay in Pawnee
jokes.punchline: The twist on 'going to hell in a handbasket' — it's a Gucci knock-off, not genuine Gucci — adds a class-conscious absurdity
jokes.explanation: The twist on a cliché is genuinely original — it's not just 'Gucci handbag' but 'Gucci knock-off,' which both preserves the wordplay rhythm and adds a layer of Pawnee-specific tackiness. 'Girl' as a kicker is character-specific. Quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Argo! Yes, I saw that. Well, I saw parts of it. I fell asleep twice, but I definitely caught the gist. Ben Affleck is really good at... being in movies.

jokes.text: Dennis supports Leslie, saying she saved his business. Leslie: 'No need for further questions on that one.' Reporter asks what his business is. Dennis: 'Oh, I run a pornographic DVD emporium.'
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to cut off questions after a supporter praises her
jokes.punchline: The supporter turns out to be a porn shop owner — the best possible person Leslie could have vouching for her in a public forum
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom structure: Leslie's attempt to cut off a line of questioning guarantees the worst possible answer. The setup (Leslie's 'no need for further questions') is what makes the punchline land. The timing is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay everyone, I have some exciting news. We just received a buyout offer for Gramercy Beverage Company. And you'll never guess who it's from.

dialogue.speaker: Someone
dialogue.line: Who?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Diddy.

dialogue.speaker: Someone
dialogue.line: It's not Diddy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's definitely Diddy. Diddy's getting into the beverage game.

dialogue.speaker: Someone
dialogue.line: Tom, we looked into it. It's not Diddy. It's a holding company out of Delaware.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's what Diddy would say.

jokes.text: Brandi Maxxxx introduces herself with her porn film titles: 'A Good Guy to Lay Hard' (Die Hard) and 'Our Goo' (Argo). 'I had a small part in Argo as well as the porn version, Our Goo.'
jokes.setup: Brandi is introducing herself at the public forum
jokes.punchline: Each film title is a pornographic pun on an Oscar-winning film; 'Our Goo' for Argo is the weakest pun but she defends it with her cameo claim
jokes.explanation: 'A Good Guy to Lay Hard' is a solid pun; 'Our Goo' is deliberately terrible in a funny way. The claim that she also had a 'small part' in actual Argo is a great detail — either she's lying or somehow true.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I'm about to treat myself so hard right now.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I'm gonna get a massage, a facial, a deep conditioning treatment, and a new weave.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Then I'm gonna get a Swedish massage, a Thai massage, a hot stone massage, and a Shiatsu massage.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Then I'm gonna go to that place in the Dominican Republic where they use volcanic rocks and the tears of angels.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: And then I'm gonna have someone feed me grapes while I get a foot massage from a dude who only does feet and has won multiple awards for his foot massage technique.

jokes.text: Ben: 'I've seen the first 90 seconds. It's thrilling.'
jokes.setup: Brandi Maxxxx has introduced her porn film 'Our Goo'
jokes.punchline: Ben has seen 90 seconds of it — specifically 90 seconds — and describes it as 'thrilling,' which is either deadpan mockery or accidental sincerity
jokes.explanation: The specificity of '90 seconds' — not 'a little' or 'some' — implies Ben started watching and then stopped at an exact point, which raises more questions than it answers. Maximum economy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: April, I need your advice about the business. What should I do?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Have you tried not wearing pants to work? It really opens up your hip flexors.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's... completely unrelated.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Also, you should definitely not report those cash transactions to the IRS. Nobody checks small businesses anyway.

jokes.text: Andy (as Macklin) interrupts Leslie's press conference to wave a pregnancy test at her, saying 'Did you or did you not leave this positive pregnancy test in a dumpster in the woods?'
jokes.setup: Leslie is in the middle of a public press conference/forum dealing with a recall threat
jokes.punchline: Andy barges in with a pregnancy test investigation at the worst possible moment, treating personal matters as a public FBI case

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: You know, I've been thinking about your relationship problems, and I have some advice.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hard pass.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: But I haven't even—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We said no.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Okay.

jokes.text: Tom's investment announcement: 'Someone — I'm not saying Diddy, but I'm not not saying Diddy — has offered to buy out Rent-A-Swag for a buttload of money.'
jokes.setup: Tom is presenting the buyout offer to his investors
jokes.punchline: 'I'm not not saying Diddy' — a double negative that means nothing legally but implies everything Tom wants — is the Diddy gag returning

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, is Mona-Lisa pregnant? Because if she is, that's... that's actually great news for me.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: My girlfriend said if Mona-Lisa got pregnant, she'd break up with me. So... fingers crossed.

jokes.text: Donna immediately: 'Sell, baby.' Then: 'Imagine the kind of treat-yourself day we could have with the profits. I'm talking pedicures on pedicures on pedicures.'
jokes.setup: Tom presents a major business decision
jokes.punchline: Donna's entire financial calculus reduces to pedicure stacking

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Look at this pregnancy test brand. It's called 'Answer.'

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, so you pee on it and it gives you the answer.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know, but the way they're marketing it... it's like they're saying 'Hey, do you have a question?' And the answer is... you're pregnant.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's how pregnancy tests work, Andy.

jokes.text: Ron's business advice: 'I say you continue to grow, accumulate power, find this investor, and buy his business to teach him a lesson.'
jokes.setup: Tom is weighing whether to sell or keep growing
jokes.punchline: Ron's advice escalates from normal business counsel to 'destroy your enemy' without changing tone
jokes.explanation: Ron's advice as a free market capitalist naturally escalates to corporate warfare. 'Buy his business to teach him a lesson' is delivered as completely reasonable strategic advice. Good character voice.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. You're pregnant? Like, actually pregnant? With a baby?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God, oh my God, oh my God. This is really happening. We're going to be parents. We're going to be... parents.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And not just us. Everyone. Everyone is someone's child. Everyone in the world is someone's child. Do you realize that? Do you understand the implications?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Billions of people. Billions of parents who thought they knew what they were doing. And they didn't. None of them did. They still don't.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh God, what if we're terrible at this? What if everyone is terrible at this? What if humanity is just a series of people doing their best and completely failing?

jokes.text: April's advice: 'I actually think that you should get a Hello Kitty tattoo.' Then, asked about the store: 'Burn it for the insurance money.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is giving Tom business advice
jokes.punchline: April gives advice about a tattoo first (completely ignoring the context), then when redirected, immediately suggests arson
jokes.explanation: April's two-beat joke — being generically weird first, then immediately criminal when redirected — is reliable April comedy. 'Burn it for the insurance money' is a specifically April escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Leslie, I need to tell you something important.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What is it, Chris?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I've been offered a position. As the Duke of Eagleton.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, what? Duke of Eagleton?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: No, actually, I'm sorry—I misspoke. It's the Countess of Soft Pretzels.

jokes.text: Gary begins to offer advice; everyone cuts him off. 'God, nobody cares, Gary.' Ben: 'Enough.' Gary: 'Thank you.' Ben: 'I miss you guys.'
jokes.setup: Gary is trying to participate in the group discussion
jokes.punchline: Gary thanks Ben for cutting off the dismissal of him, but Ben's actual statement ('I miss you guys') reveals he was talking to Chris on the phone, not defending Gary
jokes.explanation: The Gary running gag of being dismissed is elevated here by the double-layered punchline — Gary thinks he has an ally, but Ben was just on the phone. Good structure.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm the Grand Marshal of the parade.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: It's gonna be great. I've got this sash, I've got this hat, I've got this horse...

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm basically the Duke of Pawnee for the day.

jokes.text: Chris on the phone: 'Last one to pick up 100 rusty cans has still accomplished a great deal.'
jokes.setup: Chris is trying to rally the team for volunteer cleanup work
jokes.punchline: His attempt at competitive motivation completely undermines itself — there's no loser, everyone wins, even last place 'has still accomplished a great deal'
jokes.explanation: This is quintessential Chris Traeger — his compulsive positivity directly undercuts the competitive structure he's trying to create. It's only revealed at the end of the sentence, which is good structural placement. The specificity of '100 rusty cans' is excellent. Justifies 8+ on character integration — only Chris could destroy his own competition mid-sentence.

dialogue.speaker: Anti-Leslie Float Chanter
dialogue.line: Leslie Knope is bad! Leslie Knope is bad!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: What? No... that's not... that's a parade float.

jokes.text: Ben and Leslie talking-head: 'Parades and your butt: My two vices.' — Leslie attributing parades and Ben's butt as her two guilty pleasures in the same breath
jokes.setup: Ben is cheering Leslie up about the recall by mentioning parades, which she loves
jokes.punchline: Leslie equates 'parades' and 'your butt' as equivalent pleasures, completely naturally
jokes.explanation: The parallel construction — parades and a body part — delivers the punchline entirely through juxtaposition and economy. Leslie's deadpan earnestness makes it work.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Hey Leslie, don't let this get you down. You know, even Abraham Lincoln had people who didn't like him.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Yeah, and he's on the penny. You're not even on a penny yet, so... you've got room to grow!

jokes.text: Ben's arm gesture causes Leslie to call him out: 'Babe — babe, stop wagging your finger.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is stopping the parade float to protest her recall.
jokes.punchline: Ben, presumably gesturing along with her speech, is called out for 'wagging his finger' — a visual gag inferred from Leslie addressing it mid-speech.
jokes.explanation: Inferred visual gag — Ben presumably mirroring Leslie's gestures unhelpfully. Functional but not especially clever from the transcript alone.

dialogue.speaker: Crowd
dialogue.line: Leslie! Leslie! Leslie!

dialogue.speaker: Random Person
dialogue.line: TAX THE RICH!

jokes.text: Ben tells Tom the pregnancy test is 'Womb There It Is.' Tom: 'That's her brand.'
jokes.setup: Ben is showing Tom a pregnancy test to see if Mona-Lisa might be pregnant
jokes.punchline: The pregnancy test brand is named 'Womb There It Is' (a pun on 'Bomb There It Is' / '2 In a Room'); Tom immediately recognizes it as Mona-Lisa's specific brand
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. 'Womb There It Is' is a genuinely clever pun with perfect sound-match to 'Bomb There It Is.' But the real kicker — 'That's her brand,' implying Mona-Lisa has a specific pregnancy test brand she uses regularly — layers two jokes in seven words. The implication (Mona-Lisa takes enough pregnancy tests to have a preferred brand) is devastating character comedy. Highly quotable. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's mine.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Sweet Lincoln's green ass!

jokes.text: Tom: 'I'm gonna be a dad? I'm gonna have a baby with Jean-Ralphio's sister? Oh, God. What have I done? Like, to humanity?'
jokes.setup: Tom realizes Mona-Lisa might be pregnant with his child
jokes.punchline: His concern escalates from personal ('what have I done') to civilizational ('to humanity') — framing himself as a threat to the species
jokes.explanation: The escalation to 'to humanity?' is the key beat. Tom's narcissism manifests as cosmic responsibility — he's not just worried about himself, he's worried about what this DNA combination means for the human race. Strong character and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: I'm pregnant.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: Just kidding! You should see your faces! Hahahaha!

jokes.text: Chris arrives at the parade and reveals he is the 'Nipple King' of Kernston's Rubber Nipple Company.
jokes.setup: Chris has hinted at a 'special role' in the parade
jokes.punchline: The title 'Nipple King' and the company 'Kernston's Rubber Nipple Company' — both the absurdity of the business and the title — pay off the mystery
jokes.explanation: The Nipple King reveal is satisfying because of how earnestly Chris receives the honor ('It's such an amazing honor') and the specificity of 'Kernston's Rubber Nipple Company.' The juxtaposition of Chris's sincere joy with an absurd title is classic Parks and Rec.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa Saperstein
dialogue.line: I can't be pregnant. I take like, 40 pills a day. And they're not prenatal vitamins, they're just regular pills. I don't even know what they do.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa Saperstein
dialogue.line: Plus, I specifically told my doctor I only want a human baby. So if it's not human, the deal is off.

jokes.text: Leslie sees a parade float mocking her — 'No fun for you!' — and is told 'Maybe it's not you. Maybe it's Kate Upton.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is watching the Founder's Week parade and sees a float attacking her
jokes.punchline: Ben's weak attempt to suggest the 'No fun for you' float might be about Kate Upton is obviously absurd, and even he doesn't believe it
jokes.explanation: Ben's desperate attempt to comfort Leslie by suggesting the float could be about a famous model is funny in its futility. Leslie's 'Oh, thank you' followed by 'No, it's me' is a well-timed reality check.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: What's wrong with you being happy?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Your sister is terrible.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Oh my God, she is! Congratulations, man!

jokes.text: Leslie stops the parade to argue with a float: 'I am an extremely fun person!'
jokes.setup: Leslie is watching a 'No fun for you' float about her
jokes.punchline: She stops the parade to defend her fun-ness to the town — an act that is definitionally not fun
jokes.explanation: The irony is well-constructed: arguing that you are fun in the most un-fun way possible. Very Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April can't be pregnant. We have sex every day. I read on the internet that if you have sex every day, you can't get pregnant.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's not how it works.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, that's what it said. 'If you have sex every day, you won't get pregnant.' I'm pretty sure I'm reading that right.

jokes.text: The float reveals: 'We are the committee to recall Leslie Knope.' Recall Knope chants begin, then immediately followed by a lone voice: 'Legalize weed!'
jokes.setup: A dramatic recall announcement is made at the parade
jokes.punchline: Amid the serious political chant, one person takes the opportunity to advocate for an unrelated cause
jokes.explanation: The lone 'Legalize weed!' in the middle of the political chant is a perfectly timed absurdist interruption. Good economy — the joke is entirely in the context.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, we're on vacation. You need to relax.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I am relaxed! I'm just checking my email, returning some calls, drafting a few memos, and reorganizing the Parks Department's filing system remotely.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's not relaxing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It is if you love your job!

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio: 'Oh, my God, are you serious? I'm gonna be an uncle? Is that a real thing? Is that gonna happen? No, no, that's too much — too much responsibility for me. I gotta find another way out of this.'
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio learns his sister might be pregnant
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio's panic about being an uncle — a passive role requiring nothing — escalates to looking for an 'out,' treating unclehood as a burden to escape
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio panicking about the responsibilities of being an uncle is perfectly character-specific. The escalation from disbelief to 'I need to find a way out of this' is great.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You want to recall me? Fine. But let me tell you something about Leslie Knope. I don't break under pressure. I don't fold. I don't—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Footloose. Flashdance. Dirty Dancing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm thinking of dance movies. Why am I thinking of dance movies?

jokes.text: Tom starts planning a responsible future, then Mona-Lisa: 'Psych! Ah, ha, ha. Look at your stupid face. You had a dumdum face.' Then she sings '♪ That's hilarious ♪'
jokes.setup: Tom has been emotionally processing a potential pregnancy and planning responsibly
jokes.punchline: Mona-Lisa was faking the pregnancy as a prank, then mocks Tom's emotional response by singing about how hilarious it was
jokes.explanation: This is a brilliantly constructed payoff. Mona-Lisa faking a pregnancy purely to watch Tom's face, then singing a song about how funny his reaction was, is the most Mona-Lisa thing possible. 'Dumdum face' and the impromptu musical celebration of cruelty are exceptional character integration. The singing of '♪ That's hilarious ♪' is her crowning moment. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Is Silver Linings Playbook a dance movie? I mean, there's dancing in it, but it's not really a dance movie. Or is it? I don't know, that's what I'm asking.

jokes.text: Mona-Lisa: 'Do you know how many different pills I take, birth control or otherwise? There is no way that I could be pregnant with a human baby.'
jokes.setup: Tom asks if she's really not pregnant
jokes.punchline: 'With a human baby' — the qualifier implies other types of pregnancies are theoretically on the table, or she's just so chemically unusual that normal biology doesn't apply
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's strongest line. 'With a human baby' as a qualifier is absurdist at the highest level — it implies a non-human pregnancy is possible, or more precisely, that Mona-Lisa's pharmaceutical intake has removed her from normal biological rules entirely. The delivery is completely deadpan. The specificity, originality, economy, and character integration are all exceptional. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Does anybody have any questions?

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: Yeah, I do. Why does everyone hate me? Is it because I'm fat? My therapist says I'm sabotaging myself, but I think it's just that nobody likes me.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I... wasn't asking you that question.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio immediately: 'Thank God. Yes! Tommy has his life back! Let's go!' then to Tom: 'What the hell is wrong with you, man? That's my sister.' Tom: 'Nah! I'm just kidding, man. She's the worst. You dodged a bullet, baby. Congratulations.'
jokes.setup: Tom expresses relief that Mona-Lisa isn't pregnant
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio does a half-second performance of sibling loyalty before immediately abandoning it and celebrating with Tom

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This press conference is over.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I said this press conference is over!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Why do I sound like a substitute teacher?

jokes.text: Andy (as Macklin) narrates: 'It's not Mona-Lisa. It's not me, it's not Donna, it's not Leslie... Besides, the math doesn't add up because we only have sex every single day.'
jokes.setup: Andy is eliminating suspects in his pregnancy investigation
jokes.punchline: 'The math doesn't add up because we only have sex every single day' — treating daily sex as statistically insufficient for pregnancy is both wrong and delivered with complete confidence
jokes.explanation: This is a top-tier joke. Andy's sexual logic — that having sex every day somehow makes pregnancy less likely — delivered with complete analytical confidence is perfect character comedy. He's not bragging; he genuinely believes this disproves April as a suspect. The specificity of 'every single day' makes it funnier than 'a lot.' Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'd like to thank everyone for coming. Ben and I are excited to announce...

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, we talked about this. Just read the statement.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Right, right. But first, a dance number!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No. No dance number.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Just a quick one! Five, six, seven, eight!

jokes.text: Leslie confesses she wants to quit and move to the Bahamas to 'catch fish with homemade spears.' Ben: 'Yeah, you'd last about 30 seconds with that work. When we went to Hawaii, you woke me up at 3:00 A.M. to watch Meet the Press.' Leslie: 'Well, it was Elizabeth Warren. Like, I'm not going to watch that live?'
jokes.setup: Leslie fantasizes about quitting politics
jokes.punchline: Her idea of island living is immediately debunked by the anecdote that she woke Ben at 3 AM in Hawaii to watch political TV — she can't escape who she is, and her defense of it is that Elizabeth Warren is worth it
jokes.explanation: This is a standout joke for character integration. Leslie's fantasy of leaving politics is destroyed in one specific, true-to-character anecdote: she could be in Hawaii and would still prioritize live political TV. Her defense — 'It was Elizabeth Warren. Like, I'm not going to watch that live?' — is the punchline that makes this exceptional. It's not just a joke about Leslie's obsession; it's a joke that shows she has no regrets about it. Could only be delivered by this character. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Things with Chris are great. We're really happy together. He's supportive, he's kind, he remembers things I tell him. It's wonderful. I think I'm going to marry him.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'When we went to Hawaii, you woke me up at 3:00 A.M. to watch Meet the Press. Well, it was Elizabeth Warren. Like, I'm not going to watch that live?'
jokes.setup: Ben suggests they move to the Bahamas and catch fish with homemade spears; Leslie says he'd last 30 seconds with that work
jokes.punchline: The specific detail that Leslie woke Ben at 3 AM in Hawaii to watch a political show — with the defense that it was Elizabeth Warren and therefore non-negotiable
jokes.explanation: Excellent character joke. The specific detail (3 AM, Hawaii, Meet the Press, Elizabeth Warren as justification) is layered with comic precision. 'Like, I'm not going to watch that live?' is a perfect Leslie Knope line — an unanswerable logic based on values entirely specific to her. High character integration; nobody else would do or say this.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I've been doing some investigation, and I have some news about the pregnancy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April is not pregnant. She's just fat.

jokes.text: Leslie continuing to cite dance movie titles: 'Go crazy. You Got Served. Silver Linings Playbook, kind of.'
jokes.setup: Leslie's press conference continues; the dance movie title bit is now established.
jokes.punchline: 'Silver Linings Playbook, kind of' — she's running out of pure dance movies and trying to stretch the category, evidenced by her qualifier 'kind of.'
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the running gag is well-managed: the bit was established, now we're in the phase where the titles get more tenuous. 'Kind of' is the perfect hedge for Silver Linings Playbook being not quite a dance movie. The bit has good momentum through this episode.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you're pregnant! This is the best day of my life! I'm gonna be a godfather!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm not pregnant, Andy. I just got really drunk last night and ate a lot of pizza.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh.

jokes.text: Leslie's press conference speech devolves into dance movie titles after saying 'Bring it on': 'Step Up 2: The Streets... Stomp the Yard... You Got Served... Silver Linings Playbook, kind of.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is delivering an impassioned response to the recall threat
jokes.punchline: Her adrenaline produces only dance movie titles — she's aware of it, apologizes, and then keeps doing it
jokes.explanation: The running escalation of dance movie titles — and Leslie's self-aware but helpless continuation of the gag — is a great bit. 'Silver Linings Playbook, kind of' is the best beat because it's a stretch and she knows it. Good character voice: Leslie's brain works in pop culture references under stress.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm not interested in being pregnant. I'd rather adopt a baby from a country we've been at war with for a really long time, raise it as my own, and then take it back to that country and abandon it there when it turns 18.

jokes.text: Reporter: 'I think I'm better off. I haven't had a date in a while, but I'm learning a lot about me.' Leslie: 'Well, I wasn't asking you specifically, but I'm happy to hear that, Shauna.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks the crowd if they're better off
jokes.punchline: The reporter interprets a rhetorical civic question as a personal inquiry and shares her dating life update; Leslie graciously absorbs the overshare
jokes.explanation: Good use of Shauna's character (the reporter who is friendly with Leslie but usually awkward). The punchline is Leslie's gracious 'I wasn't asking you specifically, but I'm happy to hear that' — a sentence that shouldn't need to exist.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: They've copied Tom's exact business model, down to every demographic category.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, they copied my idea?

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: Completely. It's blatant.

jokes.text: Leslie tries to end her press conference with 'Recall, shmecall.' then immediately: 'No, I can't end my big press conference by saying Recall, shmecall. That's ridiculous.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is wrapping up her press conference with a defiant statement
jokes.punchline: She realizes in real time that her closing line is terrible and says so out loud
jokes.explanation: The self-correction is funny because Leslie simultaneously commits to the line (saying it) and rejects it (calling it ridiculous). Good meta-awareness from the character without breaking the show's reality.

dialogue.speaker: Trevor
dialogue.line: I'm going to destroy you in court. You'll be like a house of cards in a hurricane.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: A house of cards would actually be fine in a hurricane. It's wind, not water. Houses of cards fail in water.

jokes.text: Ben steps in to end the press conference, then Leslie: 'Thanks, honey. Honey. That's another dance movie with Jessica Alba.'
jokes.setup: Ben professionally ends the press conference
jokes.punchline: Leslie, still in adrenaline mode, identifies 'Honey' as a dance movie — a callback to her earlier dance movie gag

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: These businesses keep copying my ideas. They steal from me constantly.

dialogue.speaker: Trevor
dialogue.line: Well, I have a free lesson that will cost you.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What? That doesn't make any sense.

jokes.text: Ben lifts Ann up, declaring 'My wife is pregnant!' — Ann immediately corrects him and says she's not pregnant. Ben: 'Wait, are you sure you're not?' Ann: 'Yeah. We've talked about this. Remember? I wanna wait until we're 50 and then adopt a set of creepy adult twins from Romania.'
jokes.setup: Ben has apparently deduced Ann is pregnant (incorrectly)
jokes.punchline: Ann reveals their agreed-upon plan: wait until 50, adopt creepy adult twins from Romania — which is so specific and weird it can only be Ann's actual plan
jokes.explanation: The 'creepy adult twins from Romania' is a genuinely original and specific piece of absurdist comedy. The specificity of 'adult twins' (not children), 'Romania' (not just 'abroad'), and 'creepy' (she's not even romanticizing it) makes this a standout. Ben having heard and agreed to this plan is the extra layer. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm telling you, I have a connection to Diddy. My lawyer confirmed it.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: I said you have a connection to *ditty*, like a little song.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's basically the same thing.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Actually, there is something I need to tell you.' Ben immediately: 'You're pregnant.' Ron: 'No.' Ben: 'No!' Ron: 'We just ruled that out.' Ben: 'Ah, dang it.'
jokes.setup: Ron says he has something to tell Ben
jokes.punchline: Ben has been so marinated in the pregnancy investigation that his first guess for any secret is 'you're pregnant' — even for Ron Swanson

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: Mr. Brandanowitz, we've recovered emails showing you attended several of Mr. Combs' parties in the early 2000s.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, what? No, I didn't—

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: In fact, here's a photo of you in a white suit next to him at the—

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, yes, fine, I went to like two parties, but I barely remember them!

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: So you do admit to attending Mr. Combs' events?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No! I mean, yes, but— I was just there for the shrimp!

jokes.text: Ron and Ann discussing wanting to wait to adopt 'a set of creepy adult twins from Romania.'
jokes.setup: Ron is insisting Ann is pregnant; she says they've discussed wanting to wait.
jokes.punchline: The plan they've apparently agreed on: wait until they're 50, then adopt adult twins from Romania — specifically described as 'creepy.'
jokes.explanation: This is among the episode's best jokes. Every specific word matters: not just 'adopt twins' but 'adult twins' (why?), not just 'adult twins' but 'creepy adult twins' (who describes future children that way?), and 'from Romania' (why the specificity?). This reads as an entirely sincere Ron Swanson plan. The joke is fully character-integrated — it's exactly the kind of unsentimental, strange-specific life plan Ron would develop and Ann would apparently go along with. Strong 8+ justified by originality, character integration, and the work done by each modifier.

jokes.text: Ann reveals she got into veterinary school. Ben: 'as I've known about you for the past 20 seconds, this is your dream.'
jokes.setup: Ann shares the vet school news as a long-delayed secret
jokes.punchline: Ben's encouragement is delivered with a comically precise timestamp — he's been enthusiastically supportive for exactly 20 seconds
jokes.explanation: Ben's sincere support qualified by the exact time he's known about the dream ('20 seconds') is a sweet-funny blend that works well. Good economy.

jokes.text: Tom tells the lawyer he won't sell. Tom: 'you can go tell your client he now has 100 problems?' Lawyer: 'Is it Jay-Z?' Lawyer: 'No.'
jokes.setup: Tom paraphrases the Jay-Z lyric 'I got 99 problems' as a threat
jokes.punchline: The lawyer, who has been rigorously denying celebrity clients all episode, breaks pattern and asks if it's Jay-Z — then catches himself

jokes.text: The lawyer reveals the competitor's store is called 'Tommy's Closet' and will serve 'teens, tweens, and pres, as well as babies, toddlers, grown-ups, and olds.'
jokes.setup: The lawyer describes the competitor's planned store
jokes.punchline: The store covers every demographic ('babies, toddlers, grown-ups, and olds') — it's Tom's entire business concept with his name — and 'olds' as the senior demographic category is the kicker

jokes.text: Lawyer: 'So I guess only Domino's is allowed to sell pizza now? It's called capitalism, Mr. Haverford, and you are about to get a free lesson. Only this free lesson is going to cost you.'
jokes.setup: Tom protests that the competitor is stealing his concept
jokes.punchline: The lawyer delivers a dramatic capitalism lecture that immediately undercuts itself: 'a free lesson... only this free lesson is going to cost you'
jokes.explanation: The self-defeating 'free lesson that will cost you' is a well-structured verbal trap. The lawyer's momentary confusion ('You're right. That was confusing.') followed by steamrolling forward is great.

jokes.text: Tom: 'So it's not free?' Lawyer: 'You're right. That was confusing. This lesson will cost you. Good day.'
jokes.setup: The lawyer said 'a free lesson that costs you'
jokes.punchline: He acknowledges the contradiction, corrects himself with no loss of dignity, and exits

jokes.text: Tom: 'This sucks, but I have to admit: it's a pretty baller move. You sure this isn't Diddy?'
jokes.setup: Tom has just been outmaneuvered by the mystery investor
jokes.punchline: Even after conceding the business point, Tom circles back to the Diddy theory

jokes.text: Lawyer: 'It is Diddy.' Tom: 'I knew it!' Lawyer: 'It's not Diddy.'
jokes.setup: The Diddy gag has been running all episode
jokes.punchline: The lawyer breaks and confirms it's Diddy, then immediately takes it back — one last tease
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best running gag payoff. The lawyer — who has maintained rigid professional confidentiality all episode — finally cracks, confirms it's Diddy, then immediately takes it back. The structure is nearly perfect: it gives Tom (and the audience) exactly what they want for one beat, then denies it. 'It is Diddy.' / 'I knew it!' / 'It's not Diddy.' is three lines of maximum economy delivering a fully satisfying comedy arc. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Ron's talking head about change: 'All I care about is that I'm the same. If I'm the same as I was a year ago, I'm happy.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been asking everyone if they're 'better off' — the episode's thesis question
jokes.punchline: Ron subverts the entire question's premise: he doesn't want to be better off, just the same
jokes.explanation: Ron's answer is a perfect character encapsulation. The joke is that he's philosophically opposed to the improvement Leslie champions — not out of negativity but out of a settled satisfaction with who he is. The economy is excellent. Only Ron Swanson would answer 'are you better off?' with a sincere preference for stasis. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Andy suddenly remembers: 'Wait, I forgot. Who the hell is pregnant?' — after the entire investigation subplot
jokes.setup: Andy has been investigating the pregnancy mystery all episode as Bert Macklin
jokes.punchline: He has completely forgotten what he was doing — and remembers only after the investigation is effectively over

tmdb_overview: Leslie celebrates her first year as a city councilwoman. Retired Special Agent Burt Macklin is recalled to action. April gets some life-changing news. Tom debates a big business opportunity.
insight: Season finale sustains 2.46 jokes per minute through character chemistry alone.
